summary.text: A derangement is a permutation of a set in which no element appears in its original position.
The number of derangements of n items is the subfactorial of n, which for n > 0 equals the nearest integer to n!/e.
Counting them is the hat-check problem: returning n hats to n people so that nobody receives their own hat.

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: Montmort first considered counting them in 1708

facts.label: Small case
facts.value: A set of four members has only 9 derangements

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: The nearest integer to n!/e, for n > 0

facts.label: Hardness
facts.value: Deciding whether a permutation group has one is NP-complete

items.prompt: A teacher hands four graded tests back to four students at random. For which outcome would the handing back count as a derangement?

options.label: Exactly one student gets their own test
No student gets their own test
Every student gets their own test
At least one student gets their own test

items.explain: In a derangement no element is in its original position. Every other permutation of the four lets at least one student get their own test back.

items.prompt: In a shuffle, card 2 stays in slot 2 while every other card moves to a new slot. Is this shuffle a derangement?

options.label: Yes, because most of the cards moved
Yes, because one card staying is allowed
No, because a card stayed in its original place
No, because derangements must reverse the order

items.explain: A derangement has no fixed points, so a single card remaining in its original position rules it out.

items.prompt: With 50 people getting hats back at random, what happens to the chance that nobody gets their own hat if you grow the party to 100 people?

options.label: It barely changes, since it settles to a limit very quickly
It roughly halves, since there are twice as many people
It falls to nearly zero, since more people means more matches
It rises to nearly one, since more hats means fewer matches

items.explain: The probability converges to its limit extremely quickly as n increases, which is why Dₙ is the nearest integer to n!/e.

items.prompt: For a set of 4, the factorial is 24. Dividing 24 by e, about 2.718, gives roughly 8.83. Using the nearest-integer rule, how many derangements does a set of 4 have?
items.explain: The number of derangements is the nearest integer to n!/e, which rounds 8.83 to 9, matching the 9 derangements of a four-member set.

items.prompt: In the ménage problem, couples sit around a table alternating man and woman. What condition turns it into a constrained permutation problem?

options.label: Nobody may sit next to their partner
Everyone must sit next to their partner
No two men may know each other
Each couple must sit in alphabetical order

items.explain: The ménage problem asks how many ways couples can be seated so that nobody is seated next to his or her partner, an example of the wider field of constrained permutations.

items.prompt: A mathematician writes !n for the number of ways n hats can be returned so that nobody gets their own. What is this number called?

options.label: A binomial coefficient
Euler's number
The subfactorial
A fixed-point count

items.explain: The number of derangements of a set of size n is also called the subfactorial of n, and !n is one common notation.
